newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angola sees riches in UNITA diamond areas.
newsitem.headline: Angola sees riches in UNITA diamond areas.

text.p: Angola's government could increase diamond production by 70 percent in areas wrested from the control of former rebel movement UNITA, one of the country's diamond chiefs said on Monday.

Control over Angola's diamond areas is unfinished business between the former foes trying for peace under a unity government after two decades of civil war. The government, trying to force UNITA to hand over its diamond areas, has sent its army into the northeast.
"If they free the areas we can increase production by up to 70 percent," Paulino Neto, diamond administrator of the state-run Endiama diamond firm, told Reuters in an interview.
The government says its forces' actions are aimed at Hutu militias from the former Zaire. Western diplomats say this is a pretext to retake diamond land.

Neto, Endiama's former director-general, said the diamond sector could not grow while UNITA held 80 percent of all diamond land. He said legal production of diamonds by Endiama in 1996 totalled around $65 million, adding that illegal production was much higher.
Mining analysts estimate that UNITA earns up to $600 million annually from diamonds.

"Until this moment Endiama controls about 20 percent of areas. Practically 80 percent of all areas are outside the control of the government and the volume of diamonds that leave the country illegally is more than the diamonds controlled officially," Neto said.
He estimated that the government's diamond production share would grow in 1997 by about 30 percent as the state extended its control into UNITA areas under terms of a 1994 peace treaty.
Neto denied Endiama was in talks with UNITA over the diamond wealth, but said there had been an agreement with the UNITA-linked SGM company.

Talks between Endiama and SGM led to an agreement on two diamond concessions, passed by cabinet recently. The concessions are around UNITA's stronghold in Andulo in central Angola, and in the southern Cuando Cubango province.
There was nothing stopping SGM from negotiating with other companies for diamond partnerships, Neto said.
"There does not exist on the part of Endiama, and I believe not even on the part of the government, any impediment stopping companies discussing partnerships with SGM," he said.

Endiama is awaiting conclusion of talks between SGM and a consortium of Brazil's Odebrecht, Australia's Ashton Mining and and Endiama for a stake in diamond production royalties from a concession in the northeast, which includes UNITA's diamond mine at Lusamba.
SGM is also interested in a concession of the International Defence and Security company in the northern Cuango.
Foreign diamond interests in Angola have surged in the past year, Neto said, adding that the total value of overseas investment was unknown.

However, the start of production at the country's first kimberlite diamond mine, operated by Odebrecht at Catoca, has been delayed by two months as a convoy carrying equipment to the mine in Angola's northeast returned to Luanda amid security fears.
Pospecting by diamond giant De Beers for new kimberlites in the northeast was going ahead, Neto said, adding that the first sample from testing had been sent to Kimberley in South Africa.
